## Run it!
This charts the amount of the tip,  the total bill,  if the person was a smoker or nonsmoker, and the size of the party. [see the tabular data](https://github.com/mwaskom/seaborn-data/blob/master/tips.csv)

```{python}
# Import seaborn
import seaborn as sns

# Apply the default theme
sns.set_theme()
sns.set_style('whitegrid')

# Load an example dataset
tips = sns.load_dataset("tips")
# Note, you could also load this from your dataframe!

# Create a visualization
sns.relplot(
    data=tips, 
    x="total_bill", y="tip", col="time",
    hue="smoker", style="smoker", size="size",
    legend="auto"
)
```

## But, what?

## But wait!
On the [docs](https://seaborn.pydata.org/generated/seaborn.objects.Jitter.html) page, it shows `so.Plot` in addition to `sns.relplot`.  

```{python}
import seaborn.objects as so
# Same (ish) viz of the tips
(
    so.Plot(tips, x="total_bill", y="tip", color="smoker")
    .add(so.Dots())
    .facet(col="time")
)
```

## But wait, again
We can chain these together and stack them until we get what we want. 

```{python}
import seaborn.objects as so
# Same (ish) viz of the tips
(
    so.Plot(tips, x="total_bill", y="tip", color="smoker")
    .add(so.Dots())
    .facet(col="time")
   # .add(so.Line(alpha=.5), so.PolyFit(order=2))  # Statistical transform + mark combined
   # .add(so.Dots(alpha=0.5), so.Dodge())               # Raw data points jittered/dodged
   # .add(so.Line(), so.Agg("mean"), so.Dodge())        # Line connecting group means
    #.add(so.Range(), so.Est(errorbar="se"), so.Dodge()) # Standard error range bars
    .label(
        x="Total Bill ($)",
        y="Tip ($)",
        title="Tip vs. Bill by Time of Day"
    )
)
```
